documents.abstract: Objective: To assess the attitudes and perceptions of healthcare professionals (HCPs) towards digital health technologies (DHT).Methods: A 4-week, cross-sectional study was conducted in a tertiary care teaching hospitalin Southern India. A 14-item, self-administered questionnaire was developed and validated (kappa > 0.74). Data were collected through an online survey of HCPs available at the study site. The survey included questions related to demographics, DHT usage, and attitudes and perceptions toward DHTs. Data are presented as n (%), and odds ratio at 95% confidence intervals were used to identify predictors.Results: Among 151 participants, the mean age was 28.19 ± 7.01 years, where [81 (53.64%)]were females. Most of them [78 (51.65%)] were doctors, followed by [45 (29.8%)], [15 (9.93%)], and [13 (8.61%)] were allied healthcare professionals, nurses, and pharmacists, respectively. [129 (85.43%)] of the participants were aware of the term “digital health technologies” and [65 (43.05%)] used DHTs such as smart watches, mHealth, etc. for their health monitoring. Approximately 77% of participants were willing to adopt DHTs in their practice. However, 64% of the participants were concerned about data privacy and security issues associated with the use of DHTs. The majority (81%) of them had never undergone any formal training on digital technology or artificial intelligence in healthcare, and approximately 48% of HCPs were not sure about the patients’ perspectives on whether they would accept DHTs if introduced into their healthcare services. Knowledge of DHTs (p=0.003), current use in practice (p = 0.012), perceived user-friendliness (p <0.001), and years of experience (p = 0.034) were significant predictors of willingness to adopt DHTs.Conclusion: Good perceptions and positive attitudes were observed among the participants. However, providing adequate training and support and alleviating apprehensions regarding privacy and security may help to increase the integration of DHTs in the healthcare domain.

documents.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a central paradigm for improving reasoning and code generation in large language models, and GRPO-style training is widely adopted for its simplicity and effectiveness. However, an important design choice remains underexplored: how token-level policy gradient terms are aggregated within each sampled group. Standard GRPO uses sequence aggregation, while recent work has advocated token aggregation as a better alternative. We show that these two rules induce different optimization biases: token aggregation introduces sign-length coupling, while sequence aggregation implicitly downweights longer responses through sequence-level equal weighting. To address this tension, we propose \textbf{Balanced Aggregation (BA)}, a simple drop-in replacement that computes token-level means separately within the positive and negative subsets and then combines them with sequence-count-based weights. Experiments with Qwen2.5-Math-7B and Qwen3-1.7B on DAPO-17k and Polaris, evaluated on six reasoning and coding benchmarks, show that BA consistently improves training stability and final performance over standard token and sequence aggregation. Our analysis further shows that the relative effectiveness of token and sequence aggregation is largely governed by response-length variation and the positive-negative length gap, highlighting aggregation as a critical design dimension in GRPO-style RLVR.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been widely used by students to support learning across different levels of education. This phenomenological study explores how graduate students employ AI, particularly ChatGPT, in understanding academic research articles and how such use shapes their cognitive engagement and critical thinking. Conducted in a Master’s Program in English Language Education emphasizing critical reading, the study involved six purposively selected participants with varied academic backgrounds and teaching experiences. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews, classroom observations, and focus group discussions (FGD), and analyzed using Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (IPA). The findings reveal distinct patterns of AI use and cognitive engagement across participants. Some students demonstrated high autonomy and higher-order cognitive engagement at the evaluating and creating levels, while others used AI reflectively to support language comprehension and analysis. In contrast, certain participants showed strong dependency on AI, with cognitive engagement largely limited to remembering and understanding. Interpreted through Bloom’s Revised Taxonomy, the findings indicate that AI may function either as a cognitive scaffold or a cognitive constraint depending on how it is used. This study highlights the importance of fostering critical AI literacy to support autonomy, reflection, and higher-order thinking in graduate education.

documents.abstract: This paper examines how mathematics can be approached in the context of Adult Learning and education for older adults. Senior Education in university settings can become a highly motivating, engaging, and meaningful experience for senior learners. Drawing on our teaching practice at the Senior Classroom Program of Pablo de Olavide University (Spain), this study analyzes how andragogical principles such as autonomy, relevance, life experience, and intrinsic motivation can shape powerful learning environments for senior learners (i.e., over 50 years old). By focusing on real-world connections and on historical or philosophical perspectives, the teaching of mathematics may become not only more accessible but also intellectually stimulating, particularly when the classroom climate is supportive and inclusive. From this perspective, mathematical content, often perceived as abstract or disconnected from reality, can be approached as a resource for critical reflection, personal growth, and intergenerational dialog. Our analysis suggests that mathematics does not necessarily constitute a barrier for senior learners; under appropriate pedagogical conditions, it may instead function as a bridge to lifelong learning, fostering curiosity about how the surrounding world works and encouraging engagement with meaningful real-life problems.

Large-scale pre-training of Foundational Models (FM) constitutes a computationally intensive first phase for enabling AI across diverse scientific and societal applications. This first phase has positioned High-Performance Computing (HPC) facilities as indispensable backbones of "Sovereign AI" initiatives. While the massive throughput requirements of FM pre-training align with the traditional capability-oriented mission of HPC, subsequent phases of the AI lifecycle, typically referred to as fine-tuning and inference, introduce operational paradigms that can conflict with established batch-processing environments. Moreover, these phases are not computationally trivial: they often require substantial high-end compute resources while exhibiting hardware utilization patterns that differ significantly from those of pre-training. This paper addresses the architectural and strategic challenges of operationalizing a complete AI lifecycle within a national supercomputing facility. We present a hybrid cloud-native platform being developed and deployed at the Swiss National Supercomputing Centre (CSCS) that combines diskless GPU-enabled HPE Cray EX compute nodes with virtualized commodity infrastructure. Orchestrated by Kubernetes, this novel service architecture bridges the gap between HPC batch processing and service-oriented workflows. We report our initial investigations into fine-tuning pipelines and highly available inference services, analyzing the associated trade-offs while improving user productivity. Our findings offer a blueprint for enabling supercomputers to integrate "AI Factories" services and workflows, supporting AI innovations into end-to-end scientific and industrial use cases.

Antibiotic resistance is a significant threat to public health, and infections caused by antibiotic-resistant bacteria are becoming increasingly common. A major driver of resistance is inappropriate use of antimicrobials, often without a clear indication.1,2 One of the most common indications for antibiotic prescription is lower respiratory tract infections. Due to delays or a lack of pathogen identification and non-specific clinical and radiographic findings, clinicians are left without definitive evidence of the need for antibiotics, leading to their overuse.3 In the setting of diagnostic uncertainty, clinicians empirically prescribe antibacterial treatment, a pattern that reflects both rational risk management and well-documented cognitive biases. To address this uncertainty, several novel biomarkers have been studied to distinguish between viral and bacterial aetiologies, thereby improving targeted antibiotic decisions. Procalcitonin (PCT), a pro-inflammatory cytokine that is below 0.1 ng/mL in healthy individuals and upregulated in response to endotoxemia, has demonstrated clinically meaningful sensitivity and specificity in predicting bacterial infections. RCTs comparing PCT-guided antibiotic algorithms to standard management show a significant reduction in antibiotic exposure without increasing mortality or treatment failure.4–6 Despite this body of evidence for PCT use, decisions to initiate or discontinue antibiotics are not driven solely by biomarker values. Rather, they are embedded within social, organizational and psychological contexts that shape how information is interpreted and acted upon. Consistent with this viewpoint, a large prospective multicentre trial conducted in the USA did not demonstrate a reduction in antibiotic use with PCT-guided management alone, despite robust prior evidence.7 The authors noted that effective implementation of PCT may require additional educational and structural support.7 Thus, antibiotic stewardship is not solely a technical challenge of improving diagnostics but also a behavioural one. Understanding how clinicians interpret, trust and respond to biomarker-based recommendations, particularly within complex team environments, may be essential to realizing the full potential of PCT-guided stewardship. Traditional stewardship approaches, including clinical guidelines, education and the use of audit-and-feedback, have shown modest and variable effects on prescribing behaviour.8,9 PCT-guided stewardship offers a timely and individualized strategy that enables earlier discontinuation of antibiotics in patients with pneumonia. Importantly, it also aligns naturally with principles from behavioural economics, which offer complementary tools to enhance stewardship efforts without restricting clinician autonomy. Specifically, PCT-guided treatment recommendations supported by expert review can leverage clinician trust—a key determinant of risk perception and medical decision-making10,11 and support clinical judgments that are often complex and not purely rational. Thus, incorporating PCT into stewardship programmes through guided interpretation by a trusted governing body, such as an antimicrobial stewardship team, may therefore increase adherence and, as suggested by prior work, reduce unnecessary antibiotic use.12 When designing a PCT-guided stewardship intervention, several factors warrant consideration, including the type of recommendation and its presentation, the framing of stewardship messages, team structure and peer comparison. Adherence appears to vary by recommendation type, as found in an internal study at the Massachusetts General Hospital (MGH), a major teaching hospital in Boston, Massachusetts (MGH IRB 2019P000362). B·R·A·H·M·S PCT was assayed on a COBAS Roche platform located in the core lab with a turnaround time of 2 h. In this study, medical team providers followed an ASP recommendation to continue antibiotics based on PCT at 97.3% (93.3, 98.9; 144/148) of cases and completed a defined, shorter treatment duration at 96.5% (88.1, 99.0; 55/57) concordance. The recommendation to stop antibiotics after the first two PCT < 0.25 ng/mL (N = 113) was only followed in about half of the cases (47.8%; 38.8, 56.9), and a second recommendation to stop antibiotics on the subsequent day resulted in cessation of antimicrobials in 1 out of 7 patients (13.8%; 5.5, 30.6; 4/29). These data demonstrate a known asymmetry bias. Specifically, the recommendations to continue antibiotics or complete a predefined treatment course are often readily accepted, whereas advice to discontinue therapy, even when supported by repeatedly low PCT values and clinical stability, may encounter greater resistance. This asymmetry likely reflects classical status quo bias and loss aversion,13 whereby stopping antibiotics may feel riskier than continuing them, despite evidence to the contrary. These observations suggest the need to examine adherence by recommendation type and to optimize how recommendations are presented. Behavioural economics offers several promising approaches, including the use of ‘nudges’ to guide decision-making while preserving clinician autonomy. Framing effects, that is, presenting outcomes as gains rather than losses, are known to influence clinical decisions.14–17 Similarly, PCT-guided recommendations could emphasize either the harms of antibiotic overuse or the safety and benefits of discontinuing unnecessary therapy to improve adherence and decision quality. Team structure is another underappreciated determinant of stewardship effectiveness. Clinical decisions in hospital settings are frequently made by teams rather than individuals, and research in behavioural science suggests that group decision-making can both mitigate and amplify cognitive bias.18,19 Clinical team structure may differ in how they respond to stewardship recommendations, with larger, multi-clinician teams appearing more likely to adhere to and follow guidance than smaller teams or individual hospitalists. In fact, larger teams may diffuse individual responsibility and facilitate acceptance of external recommendations, whereas smaller teams or individual clinicians may rely more on personal experience and availability heuristics.20–24 Variation in adherence across team structures observed in prior stewardship initiatives raises important questions. Are larger teams more likely to follow stewardship recommendations because they engage in more deliberative, data-driven decision-making? Or does conformity to perceived consensus, sometimes described as groupthink, play a role?25 Although evidence generally suggests that groups outperform individuals in complex decision-making tasks,19,26 understanding the mechanisms underlying these effects is critical for optimizing stewardship design. Clinical decisions are shaped not only by data but also by contextual, psychological, social and emotional factors.27 Interventions tailored to individuals or smaller teams may therefore benefit from communication strategies that emphasize the effectiveness of PCT-guided recommendations or leverage social influence. Social norm feedback, for example, has been shown to reduce inappropriate antibiotic prescribing by highlighting how an individual’s behaviour compares with that of peers.9,28 Building on this approach, stewardship systems could incorporate peer comparison or consensus cues (e.g. ‘Most clinicians discontinue antibiotics at this PCT level’) to encourage adherence. Overall, stewardship strategies that fail to account for team context risk uneven uptake. A one-size-fits-all approach may succeed in some clinical settings while proving ineffective in others. In summary, biomarkers such as procalcitonin provide powerful, evidence-based guidance for antibiotic stewardship, but their impact depends critically on how clinicians engage with them. Integrating behavioural insights, including trust-based communication, strategic framing, social comparison and attention to team structure, offers a promising path to improving antibiotic decision-making while preserving clinician autonomy.29 Moving beyond the algorithm to address the human factors that underlie prescribing behaviour is essential to reducing unnecessary antibiotic use and combating antimicrobial resistance in everyday clinical practice. AI is increasingly used in high-stakes decisions; yet, it can reproduce social bias in its outputs. This study tested an end-user-facing, post-processing intervention that pairs model-agnostic counterfactual explanations with brief inoculation training to surface bias at decision time and counter automation bias. Counterfactual inoculation improved bias recognition in hiring, with the strongest effects observed for socially salient cues such as gender and ethnicity. Confidence gains were smaller and inconsistent. Trust did not rise uniformly, indicating calibrated skepticism rather than indiscriminate distrust. Counterfactual audit flags interrupted reflexive acceptance by showing how small input changes affect rankings, while inoculation primed users to look for bias signals, jointly shifting trust toward appropriate calibration. Practical implications include adding simple “what-if” audit flags that work with any model, allowing override or escalation when needed, and providing brief, hands-on training. Limitations include scenario-dependent effects, self-reported outcomes in a simulated workflow, and heteroscedasticity in a subset of models, which was addressed through Welch correction and bootstrapped Analysis of Covariance. Future research should assess durability over time, incorporate behavioral endpoint tools, extend this research to domains beyond hiring, and adapt explanation complexity to the domain and the user. In summary, an inoculation that explains the prevalence of bias in AI hiring tools, plus counterfactuals that expose bias cues offer a practical, interpretable means to make bias visible when decisions are made in and to move end-user trust in AI tools from blind acceptance to calibrated judgment.
